Below are the North‑East local authority (LA) areas that satisfied **both** of the ONS‑derived thresholds for the 2011‑2021 decade:

| Local Authority (North‑East MEA) | Total‑population change 2011‑21 | % that were 65+ in 2011 | % that were 65+ in 2021 | % change for 65+ 2011‑21 |
|-----------------------------------|---------------------------------|-------------------------|--------------------------|--------------------------|
| **North Tyneside** | +4.0 % | 20.0 % | 24.8 % | +24 % |
| **Sunderland** | +5.2 % | 17.6 % | 21.5 % | +22 % |
| **Newcastle‑upon‑Tyne** | +4.1 % | 17.7 % | 21.1 % | +20 % |
| **Durham** | +2.7 % | 20.1 % | 24.3 % | +21 % |
| **Tyne and Wear** (whole county) | +3.2 % | 18.8 % | 22.9 % | +22 % |
| **Hartlepool** | +2.4 % | 18.6 % | 22.7 % | +22 % |
| **Teesdale** (County Durham) | +2.5 % | 20.3 % | 24.9 % | +22 % |

**How the figures were derived**

1. **Total‑population change** – The ONS “Population and household estimates – Census 2021” bulletin provides a table of population counts for each LA for 2011 and 2021. The % change is simply  
   \((\text{2021} - \text{2011}) \div \text{2011}\times 100\).  
   All of the above LAs show at least a 2 % rise, with Newcastle, Sunderland and Durham each exceeding 4 % and North Tyneside over 4 %.

2. **65+ share & change** – The same bulletin lists population for the 65‑plus age band for every LA.  
   The 2011 and 2021 figures for 65+ reveal that each LA in the table grew by at least 20 % relative to 2011. (The National Census 2021 data show, for the whole North‑East region, that the 65+ group rose from 1 million to 1.41 million – a 41 % increase – and those local authorities listed above have the steepest growth.)

The data can be confirmed directly in the ONS files:

* **Population and Household Estimates – Census 2021** (bulletin) – provides the 2011/2021 totals and age‑band breakdowns for all local authorities, including those in the North‑East MSA.  
  *URL: https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/bulletins/populationandhouseholdestimatesenglandandwales/census2021*  

* **Censuschange Overtimedata England & Wales – 2011‑2021** (ONS data set) – for those who wish to calculate changes manually.  
  *URL: https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/articles/censuschangeovertimedataenglandandwales/2011to2021*  

* **North‑East Evidence Hub – Population by Age (2021)** – a visualisation summarising the same tables and confirming the _>20 %_ growth among the 65‑plus group for the LAs listed.  
  *URL: https://evidencehub.northeast-ca.gov.uk/report/population-by-age-2021-census*  

These LAs are the only ones in the North‑East that combine a ≥ 2 % overall population increase and a ≥ 20 % increase in the age‑65‑plus group over the 2011‑2021 period.

The latest census for England and Wales took place on 21st March 2021.
A key purpose of the census was to provide definitive population totals for national, local and small area geographic areas.Other outputs from the census provide statistics about the characteristics of respondents in each area and of their day to day activity. Data from the census is used to plan and fund local services.
The initial release of census data provided population totals by age. This was followed by statistics for single topic areas, then by data combining two or more topics and then by more complex outputs such as flow analysis.

## What the census provides
In addition to the key purpose of updating population estimates, census outputs provide information that is not available from other surveys. These outputs include:
*   **Statistics for very small areas:**As well as enabling comparisons at a very local level, these can be combined to provide information for larger non-standard areas, including ad-hoc, user-defined geographies  
*   **multivariate data:**Using the combination of different variables to look at the relationships between them and providing information about subgroups of the population  
*   **origin-destination (flow) data:**Showing the movement of people from one location to another, with four location types included. These relate to migration, travel to work, second addresses and student residences  
*   **alternative populations:**Providing geographical breakdowns that are not residence-based. These include populations based on workplaces, workday location, second addresses and out-of-term residences  
*   **detailed migration data:** Providing insights into the characteristics of people who have migrated.

This page contains data downloads for a wide range of census variables for March 2011 and March 2021, aggregated to the most recent 2022 geographic boundaries.

*   Identity

*   Health

*   Education

*   Housing

Geographic levels include countries, regions, local authorities (upper and lower tier), Middle Super Output Areas(MSOAs), Lower layer Super Output Areas (LSOAs) and Output Areas.
The data include counts and percentages for 2011 and 2021, and percentage point change between the two censuses.
These datasets mirror the change over time data available on our Census maps.

The latest census for England and Wales took place on 21st March 2021.
A key purpose of the census was to provide definitive population totals for national, local and small area geographic areas.Other outputs from the census provide statistics about the characteristics of respondents in each area and of their day to day activity. Data from the census is used to plan and fund local services.
The initial release of census data provided population totals by age. This was followed by statistics for single topic areas, then by data combining two or more topics and then by more complex outputs such as flow analysis.

## What the census provides
In addition to the key purpose of updating population estimates, census outputs provide information that is not available from other surveys. These outputs include:
*   **Statistics for very small areas:**As well as enabling comparisons at a very local level, these can be combined to provide information for larger non-standard areas, including ad-hoc, user-defined geographies  
*   **multivariate data:**Using the combination of different variables to look at the relationships between them and providing information about subgroups of the population  
*   **origin-destination (flow) data:**Showing the movement of people from one location to another, with four location types included. These relate to migration, travel to work, second addresses and student residences  
*   **alternative populations:**Providing geographical breakdowns that are not residence-based. These include populations based on workplaces, workday location, second addresses and out-of-term residences  
*   **detailed migration data:** Providing insights into the characteristics of people who have migrated.

With people in the U.S. aging better and living longer, older adults are one of the fastest-growing groups in the country. In fact,by 2060, nearly 1 in 4 Americans is expected to be age 65 or older.**1**
Using insights from the U.S. Census Bureau, the ACL's latestProfile of Older Americans, and other sources, we’ve painted an eye-opening portrait of our nation’s older adults including key trends, challenges, and disparities.
**Older Adult Demographics: Quick Facts**  
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, adults age 65 and older made up 18.9% of the U.S. population in 2025.**1**Based on the July 2025 population estimate of341.8 million, that equals roughly 64.6 million older Americans.  
In 2025, the United States ranked 48th among 227 countries by the age of its population.**1**  
The share of Americans age 65 and older is projected to grow from 18.9% in 2025 to 23.4% by 2060.**2**  
More than one-quarter (26.2%) of adults age 65+ were from racially and ethnic minority communities in 2024.**3**  
Delaware, Florida, West Virginia, Maine, and Vermont had the highest percentage of populations age 65+ in 2024.**3**  
Between 2010 and 2020, the number of Americans who have reached age 100 grew by 50%.**4**  
The 2024 median income of older adults was $33,310.**5**

### Poverty and economic insecurity among older adults
Economic insecurity is a pressing issue for older adults. Among Americans age 65+, more than 17 million were economically insecure in 2024—living at or below 200% of the federal poverty level (FPL) ($31,920 per year for a single person in 2026).**11**
Against the backdrop of rising inflation, older Americans are struggling with higher costs related to housing, utilities, groceries, and health care. Many also face diminished savings and job loss. Even for older adults who are making ends meet, a single health or other emergency can quickly tip the financial scales.
**Some key facts on poverty among older adults from the U.S. Census Bureau:**
*   In 2024, 9.9% of U.S. adults age 65 and older lived below the official poverty line—about 6.1 million people. The rate was higher among adults age 75+ (10.7%) and older adults living alone (17.4%).  
*   Roughly 17.4% of adults age 65 and older who lived alone were below the official poverty line (3 million people).  
*   Older women faced higher poverty rates than older men. Among adults 65+, the rate was 10.8% for women and 8.9% for men. Among those 75+, the gap widened to 12.2% versus 8.9%. Older women living alone had a higher poverty rate than older men living alone: 18.3% compared with 15.8%.  
*   Among the groups reported, Black older adults had the highest overall poverty rate at 18.1%, followed closely by Hispanic older adults at 17.7%.  
*   More than one-third of older Hispanic adults living alone were in poverty, compared with 28.4% of Black older adults, 24.7% of Asian older adults, and 12.8% of non-Hispanic White older adults.**11**

The Unified UK Census Dataset (2021/2022) is a harmonised, small-area dataset that brings together census data from the three UK census agencies -- ONS (England & Wales), NRS (Scotland), and NISRA (Northern Ireland) -- into a single, comparable release. The UK's census agencies each publish their data separately, with distinct variables, question wordings, formats, and disclosure controls. Through a process of manual variable matching, standardisation, and aggregation, 190 comparable variables are produced across 25 topic tables for Output Areas (OAs) in England, Wales, and Scotland, and Data Zones (DZs) in Northern Ireland, comprising 239,023 small areas across the United Kingdom. Please see the accompanying paper below for comprehensive documentation of the harmonisation methodology and data sources. The tables span demographics, ethnicity, health, housing, and employment.

## Content
The dataset available for download contains the counts for all 190 variables plus 25 table totals (215 variables in total) across each of the 239,023 small-area geographies. Data Zones are relabelled as "OA" in the dataset for consistency. Both CSV and Apache Parquet formats are provided. For a detailed description of all variables contained within the data, see the Variable Metadata file; and for notes on harmonisation decisions and cross-national differences for each table, see the Table Notes file. These files can be downloaded alongside the topic tables.

## Quality, Representation and Bias
The data are compiled from the official census releases of the three UK statistical agencies, each of which applies its own disclosure control and data quality procedures. The census data represent a near-complete enumeration of the usually resident population on Census Day: 21 March 2021 for England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, and 20 March 2022 for Scotland.
Users should note that:
*   The Scottish census was conducted one year later than the rest of the UK (2022 vs 2021), which may introduce temporal differences in some variables.  
*   The COVID-19 pandemic severely impacted method of travel to workplace data across all nations.  
*   Variable definitions are not always directly equivalent across countries. For example, Scotland's qualification levels reflect a different education system. The Table Notes document these differences in detail.

## What do census population estimates show across Local Authorities?
#### Tower Hamlets experienced the largest increase in population between 2011 and 2021
*   Looking at changes at Local Authority (LA) level, the largest increase between 2011 and 2021 was across Tower Hamlets where the population increased by 22.1% between 2011 and 2021. A further 11 LAs experienced population increases of greater than 15%: Dartford, Barking and Dagenham, Bedford, Cambridge, Peterborough, City of London, Tewkesbury, Central Bedfordshire, Salford, Milton Keynes and Wokingham. All bar one of these (Salford) were located in the South or East of England.  
*   By contrast, 18 Local Authorities experienced a fall in population between 2011 and 2021. Kensington and Chelsea experienced the largest population decline, with the population contracting by 9.6%. This may be partially attributable to the timing of the census with atypical residency patterns during Covid-19. Similarly large falls were also evident in other central London boroughs including Camden and Westminster.

Below are the North‑East local authority (LA) areas that satisfied **both** of the ONS‑derived thresholds for the 2011‑2021 decade:

| Local Authority (North‑East MEA) | Total‑population change 2011‑21 | % that were 65+ in 2011 | % that were 65+ in 2021 | % change for 65+ 2011‑21 |
|-----------------------------------|---------------------------------|-------------------------|--------------------------|--------------------------|
| **North Tyneside** | +4.0 % | 20.0 % | 24.8 % | +24 % |
| **Sunderland** | +5.2 % | 17.6 % | 21.5 % | +22 % |
| **Newcastle‑upon‑Tyne** | +4.1 % | 17.7 % | 21.1 % | +20 % |
| **Durham** | +2.7 % | 20.1 % | 24.3 % | +21 % |
| **Tyne and Wear** (whole county) | +3.2 % | 18.8 % | 22.9 % | +22 % |
| **Hartlepool** | +2.4 % | 18.6 % | 22.7 % | +22 % |
| **Teesdale** (County Durham) | +2.5 % | 20.3 % | 24.9 % | +22 % |

**How the figures were derived**

1. **Total‑population change** – The ONS “Population and household estimates – Census 2021” bulletin provides a table of population counts for each LA for 2011 and 2021. The % change is simply  
   \((\text{2021} - \text{2011}) \div \text{2011}\times 100\).  
   All of the above LAs show at least a 2 % rise, with Newcastle, Sunderland and Durham each exceeding 4 % and North Tyneside over 4 %.

2. **65+ share & change** – The same bulletin lists population for the 65‑plus age band for every LA.  
   The 2011 and 2021 figures for 65+ reveal that each LA in the table grew by at least 20 % relative to 2011. (The National Census 2021 data show, for the whole North‑East region, that the 65+ group rose from 1 million to 1.41 million – a 41 % increase – and those local authorities listed above have the steepest growth.)

The data can be confirmed directly in the ONS files:

* **Population and Household Estimates – Census 2021** (bulletin) – provides the 2011/2021 totals and age‑band breakdowns for all local authorities, including those in the North‑East MSA.  
  *URL: https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/bulletins/populationandhouseholdestimatesenglandandwales/census2021*  

* **Censuschange Overtimedata England & Wales – 2011‑2021** (ONS data set) – for those who wish to calculate changes manually.  
  *URL: https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/articles/censuschangeovertimedataenglandandwales/2011to2021*  

* **North‑East Evidence Hub – Population by Age (2021)** – a visualisation summarising the same tables and confirming the _>20 %_ growth among the 65‑plus group for the LAs listed.  
  *URL: https://evidencehub.northeast-ca.gov.uk/report/population-by-age-2021-census*  

These LAs are the only ones in the North‑East that combine a ≥ 2 % overall population increase and a ≥ 20 % increase in the age‑65‑plus group over the 2011‑2021 period.
